svg.aria-label: Conventional seed-chain-extend alignment: seeds are clustered into local chains that are extended and scored one at a time, so chains overlap on the read and offer competing explanations of the same read bases, which overlap rules settle only after the fact, leaving some read bases in two records.
svg.text: Conventional alignment: chains that compete for the read
Seed–chain–extend aligners build and extend each chain on its own, so chains overlap on the read and offer
competing explanations of the same bases, settled afterwards by overlap rules. The same read as in the global-chaining figure.
chain D: a repeat copy of chain A’s bases
alignments extend past the outer seeds,
two loci compete for these bases:
Schematic, not to scale; describes seed–chain–extend aligners in general.
Seeds on one chromosome and strand, close to one diagonal, are
chained within a maximum gap. A strand change, another
chromosome or a large jump ends the chain.
Extend and score each chain alone
Each chain is extended past its outer seeds and scored on its
own. Nothing stops one chain’s extension running into the bases
its neighbour explains, and nothing scores the step from one
So two chains can explain the same read bases: neighbours
overlap at their ends, and a repeat copy (chain D) competes
with the true locus (chain A) for a whole stretch of the read.
Each chain alone looks like a good explanation.
A chain mostly covered by a better one becomes secondary;
smaller overlaps survive, and those read bases appear in two
records. Which explanation wins depends on thresholds, not on
an account of the whole read.
builds one explanation of the whole read. Each read base is
credited at most once, so pieces cannot overlap, and a repeat
copy competes with the true locus inside the same chain, with
every step between pieces costed in bits.
